lead: An active call must survive when the user moves from one cell to the next. An idle phone must still be found when a call arrives. Cellular mobility management does both jobs. Handover moves an active connection to a new base station without dropping the call. Location tracking lets the network find an idle phone with low signalling. GSM and UMTS use these mechanisms every day, and later mobile networks reuse the same ideas. This chapter covers handover types and phases, the main handover signals, and the location-area method for paging.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.3 for HLR, VLR and MSC, and Chapter 1.4 for cell boundaries and reuse.

blocks.text: A cell boundary is where a neighbour base station's signal becomes stronger or cleaner than the serving base station. If the call stayed on the old cell, the link would fail. Handover moves the radio link to a new base station while the call continues. Some texts call it handoff.

Hard handover breaks the old link before making the new one. The phone retunes to a new channel, so the call is interrupted briefly. GSM uses hard handover. Soft handover makes the new link before breaking the old one. The phone talks to two base stations at once. Soft handover fits code division multiple access naturally, so WCDMA, the radio interface of UMTS, uses it. Later systems can also hold two links at once, for example dual connectivity in LTE. See Chapter 1.3.

items: Measurement: the mobile station (MS, the phone) and the base station measure signal strength and quality for the serving and neighbour cells.
Initiation: a measurement crosses a threshold, or a timer fires, so handover becomes a candidate.
Decision: the base station subsystem (BSS, base station and controller) or the mobile switching centre (MSC, the switch) chooses the target cell and the moment.
Execution: the network reserves a channel, sends the command, the MS accesses the new cell, and the old channel is released.

blocks.where: f is the fraction of call time lost; H is the number of handovers; t_b is the break per hard handover in seconds; T is the call duration in seconds.

blocks.text: The figure shows the main messages. The MS sends a measurement report to the old BSS. The old BSS sends handover required to the MSC. The MSC, with the visitor location register (VLR, a local database of subscribers in its area), sends handover request to the new BSS. The new BSS reserves a channel and returns an acknowledgement, channel ready. The MSC sends handover command to the old BSS, which forwards it to the MS. The MS sends handover access to the new BSS. The new BSS reports handover complete to the MSC. The MSC releases the old channel. Real GSM has more messages; these are the main ones.

The serving VLR (and MSC) changes only when the phone moves into a new MSC area. Inside the same MSC area the radio path moves and the stored location area in the VLR is updated, but the subscriber record is not fetched again. If the MS moves to a new MSC, the new VLR sends an update location to the home location register (HLR, the permanent subscription database). The HLR stores the new VLR address, sends the subscription data to the new VLR, and cancels the record in the old VLR. This is inter-MSC handover.
Newer cores use SDN (software-defined networking) for centralised control and NFV (network function virtualisation) to run core functions as software; the handover and location jobs stay the same.

sections.h3: Location tracking: attach, update and paging

blocks.text: An idle phone has no call, but the network must find it when a call arrives. Tracking every idle phone's exact cell would need an update at every cell change, which drains battery and loads signalling. Instead, cells are grouped into a location area (LA). An LA is a set of cells with one identity, the location area identity (LAI). The phone can move inside the LA without telling the network.

items: Attach: on switch-on, the phone registers; the VLR creates or refreshes the subscriber record.
Detach: on switch-off or SIM removal, the phone tells the network; the VLR marks the record detached or removes it.
Detect: the phone reads the broadcast LAI and finds it differs from the stored LAI.
Request: the phone sends a location update request through the new BSS to the MSC/VLR.
Update: the VLR updates the record; if the MSC changed, the HLR is told the new serving VLR address.
Acknowledge: the network returns an acknowledgement, and the phone stores the new LAI.

blocks.text: Paging is the reverse. For an incoming call, the MSC asks the VLR for the LA. The MSC sends a paging message to all cells in that LA. The phone answers, and the call is set up. A large LA makes paging expensive because many cells transmit. A small LA makes updates expensive because the phone crosses LA boundaries often. That trade-off is the core of location management.

examples.question: A call lasts 120 s. The user crosses a cell boundary every 15 s. Each hard handover breaks the link for 60 ms. Find the number of handovers, the total break time in ms and in s, the fraction of the call lost, and the percentage lost.
steps: Break per handover: t_b = 60 ms ÷ 1000 = 0.06 s.
Total break: H × t_b = 8 × 0.06 s = 0.48 s = 480 ms.
examples.answer: The call has 8 handovers, loses 480 ms in total, and the lost fraction is 0.004, which is 0.4 percent of the call time.

call_s = 120
cross_s = 15
break_ms = 60
H = call_s / cross_s
t_b = break_ms / 1000
total_s = H * t_b
total_ms = total_s * 1000
f = total_s / call_s
percent = f * 100
print(int(H))
print(int(total_ms))
print(total_s)
print(f)
print(percent)

traps: The phone does not send a location update at every cell change. It updates when it enters a new location area, plus on a periodic timer; inside the area the network pages it.
Hard is break before make (GSM); soft is make before break (WCDMA). Do not swap them.
The VLR is temporary and local to an MSC area; the HLR is the permanent home database.
Convert milliseconds to seconds before dividing by a call time in seconds: 60 ms is 0.06 s.
In the message sequence, the MS sends measurement report to the old BSS; the MSC sends handover request to the new BSS.

quiz.q: Define handover in a cellular network.
quiz.a: Handover is the process of moving an active connection from one base station to another while the call continues.
A location area is a set of cells with one identity; the network pages an idle phone in all cells of its current location area.

quiz.q: Why is soft handover used in WCDMA but not in GSM?
quiz.a: Soft handover needs the mobile to transmit to two base stations on the same frequency. WCDMA uses code division, so both links can share the frequency with different codes. GSM uses separate frequency or time channels, so it uses hard handover.

quiz.q: A call lasts 90 s. The user crosses a cell boundary every 10 s. Each hard handover breaks the link for 50 ms. Find the number of handovers, total break in ms, and percentage of call time lost.
quiz.a: H = 90 ÷ 10 = 9; total break = 9 × 50 ms = 450 ms = 0.45 s; fraction = 0.45 ÷ 90 = 0.005; percentage = 0.5 percent.

quiz.q: In the main GSM handover sequence, which entity sends handover request and which entity receives it?
quiz.a: The MSC sends handover request to the new BSS.

quiz.q: A phone moves through 20 cells inside one location area and sends no location update. Is this correct? Explain.
quiz.a: Yes. The phone updates on entering a new location area, not on every cell change. Inside the same location area the network pages all cells, so no update is needed.

quiz.q: Explain the trade-off between location area size and paging cost.
quiz.a: A large location area gives fewer updates but paging uses many cells. A small location area gives cheap paging but frequent updates, more signalling and more battery use.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real core networks use SDN to separate control from forwarding and NFV to run functions such as the MSC or VLR as software. Self-organising networks tune handover thresholds from measurements. 5G adds beam-level mobility, so a phone may switch beams inside one cell before it switches cells. Network slicing lets one physical core carry several logical networks with different mobility settings. Search next for SDN-based mobility management, NFV in the mobile core, and 5G handover.
